raw_response:
I'm 68 now, and I've worked these 20 mu for 45 years. I studied at the agricultural college back in the 1970s, so I understand the technical side — N rates, yield targets, soil fertility. But I'm also practical. At my age, I can't lift what I used to, and there's only my wife and me at home now. She works part-time at the garment factory in town, so during busy seasons I'm often alone in the field. That means I have to hire labor for the heavy work, and every yuan I spend on hired hands is a yuan I can't spend on fertilizer or keep aside for emergencies.

For winter wheat, I'll plant all 20 mu around October 12th with Jimai 26, the improved variety I've used for five years. I know from my soil test records and the county extension sheets that the book rate for 500 kg/mu wheat is about 18–20 kg N per mu, but I'm targeting 450 kg/mu this year. I'd rather leave some cash in reserve than gamble on perfect weather. My base fertilizer will be 50 kg of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu, applied before sowing. At jointing — usually late March — I'll topdress with 20 kg of urea per mu. That gives me roughly 16.7 kg N, 7.5 kg P₂O₅, and 7.5 kg K₂O per mu. For irrigation, I'll water three times: revival water in early March, jointing water in late March, and heading water in late April. The metered well water costs about 30 yuan per mu per irrigation, so three times is already 1,800 yuan for the wheat alone. I won't do a fourth unless May is extremely dry — I can't afford it, and at 68 I don't have the energy to manage extra irrigation rounds by myself.

For summer maize, the turnaround after wheat harvest is always the bottleneck. June 10th to June 16th — that's my window. I'll hire the custom combine for wheat harvest, then immediately no-till plant the maize with Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed. No time for plowing; the textbooks say minimum tillage works fine on these soils anyway, and at my age I couldn't turn 20 mu in six days even if I wanted to. For fertilizer, I'll apply 20 kg of DAP per mu at planting, then side-dress 25 kg of urea at the V6 stage. That's about 15 kg N and 9 kg P₂O₅ per mu. I'll irrigate twice — once at the big trumpet stage in July, and once at filling in August. But if the summer rains are good, I might skip the second irrigation and save the pumping cost. Cash in hand matters more than a marginal yield bump.

For pesticides, I'll spray herbicide on both crops — 2,4-D ester for wheat and atrazine for maize. For wheat, I'll also do one fungicide spray at heading if the weather looks humid; stripe rust has been a problem in wet springs, and losing 100 kg/mu to disease would hurt more than the 20 yuan for fungicide.

Labor-wise, I figure about 18 days of my own time on the wheat and 17 days on the maize — mostly management, irrigation, scouting, and light fertilizer spreading. For hired labor, I'll need about 20 days total: 10 days for the wheat harvest and maize planting rush, 6 days for maize harvest, and 4 days for heavy fertilizer application and any repair work. Hired labor is 150 yuan per day now, so that's 3,000 yuan I have to budget for.

Total input cost I'm looking at is about 20,000 yuan for the year. That's a lot for 20 mu, but it's the minimum to get a decent crop. If wheat gives me 450 kg/mu and maize gives me 500 kg/mu, and prices hold, I should clear enough to live on and keep some cash in reserve. At 68, I'm not trying to get rich — I'm trying to make sure we have enough to eat, enough to cover my wife's medicine, and enough left over so we don't have to ask our children for money.
